screens.prompt: The workbook is pinned to 15 March 2024, so put the record's age in whole months into C2.

hints.syntax: DATEDIF wants a start, an end and a unit: =DATEDIF(B2,TODAY(),"M").
hints.func-datedif: The age is a distance between two dates, and DATEDIF is the function that measures one.
hints.func-today: The end of the interval is today, so ask the clock rather than typing 15 March.
hints.require-ref: Read the opened date from B2 so the second policy follows without editing.
hints.value: January 2022 to March 2024 is 26 whole months — DATEDIF stops at the last completed month.
hints.error: Reversed dates make the interval negative, and DATEDIF refuses that with #NUM!.

screens.prompt: Pay on the last day of the month after the invoice date, so fill C2 with a formula rather than a date.

hints.syntax: EOMONTH takes the starting date and a count of months: =EOMONTH(B2,1).
hints.func-eomonth: One month after March is April, and the payment date is April's last day, not April's first.
hints.require-ref: Read the issued date from B2 rather than typing the serial, so the row keeps following the invoice.
hints.value: EOMONTH(B2,1) with B2 in March lands on 30 April 2024, serial 45412 — a 0 would give 31 March.
hints.error: Dividing by zero anywhere in the formula replaces the date with #DIV/0!.

docs.explain: This is the lesson where the date functions stop being separate tricks. The age column asks the clock what today is and measures a distance from it in whole months, so it combines TODAY, which you cannot type in twice and get right twice, with DATEDIF, which counts completed months and stops before the partial one. The payment column asks a different question — not how far apart two dates are, but where the edge of a month falls — and answers it with EOMONTH, whose second argument is a month offset: 0 is the end of this month, 1 the end of next month, and -1 the end of last month. Both formulas return a serial, so both can be arithmetic operands: add a term length to a date to get a due date, subtract one serial from another to get days, and format nothing at all, because a serial prints as a number until you ask for a date format. The recurring mistake is confusing the offset with the unit: EOMONTH counts months, DATEDIF counts whatever unit you name, and DAYS counts days only.

errors.text: DATEDIF was given an end date before its start date, so there is no positive interval to count.
EOMONTH was asked for a month offset that lands outside the range of serials, such as a year before 1900.
A date argument arrived as text that cannot be read as a date, so there is no serial underneath it.

docs.atWork: A policy register that ages every open record against today, and an invoice log that pays on the last working day of the following month, both without a single hand-typed date.
docs.outcome: Combine today, a distance and a month edge in formulas that keep working tomorrow.
docs.dataset: A policy register and an invoice payment log
